Tech S-Curve Leaders|U|Universe: Ben Silver and David Tykocinski (Maverick) state that one screen should cover software and AI picks-and-shovels alike, because value in a technology wave moves between layers, "upstream" first and downstream later. No specific past example given.
Tech S-Curve Leaders|A1|History: Alex Sacerdote states that an S-curve shows up as growth and rising margins together, because "when you get scurve and a rising margin your earnings don't grow linearly they grow exponentially"; seeing both needs several years of numbers. No specific past example given.
Tech S-Curve Leaders|A2|Recent report: Old numbers can hide a recent collapse; the screen needs the latest annual report. No specific past example given.
Tech S-Curve Leaders|A3|Size (revenue): Matches the Emerging screen's size floor: tiny filers have patchy data and are hard to own. No specific past example given.
Tech S-Curve Leaders|A4|Fast growth: Brad Gerstner states that growth means value in technology, because "the single greatest input to valuation technology is growth". No specific past example given.
Tech S-Curve Leaders|A5|Growth not fadin: Alex Sacerdote states that a revenue miss means a broken tech stock, because "the biggest reason people blow up in Tech is they miss on revenue". Brad Gerstner adds that "every sell-side model on Wall Street has linear deceleration in growth rates", so a fade faster than that surprises the market. No specific past example given.
Tech S-Curve Leaders|A6|Rule of 40 after: Philippe and Thomas Laffont (Coatue) state that growth plus profitability of 40 marks the strong cohort, because "growth in profitability yielding a rule of 40 was kind of the average of the cohort". Brad Gerstner and Bill Mylod state that stock pay is a real expense, so it is subtracted from free cash flow here. No specific past example given.
Tech S-Curve Leaders|A7|Gross margin: Aaron Levie states that a low gross margin means a software company can never earn software margins, because at "40 50 60% gross margin, like there's just like no way you're going to have an operating margin [that] looks like a software company". Maverick states that hardware is different: the "sharpest revision torque" came "frequently against companies that had very low margin basis", so for hardware the test is a rising margin. No specific past example given.
Tech S-Curve Leaders|A8|Operating levera: Alex Sacerdote states that rising margins on an S-curve mean exponential earnings, because "when you get scurve and a rising margin your earnings don't grow linearly they grow exponentially". No specific past example given.
Tech S-Curve Leaders|A9|Stock pay vs fre: Brad Gerstner states that stock pay under a fifth of free cash flow marks a rare, disciplined company, because there are "maybe 10 names that are under 20% of their free cash flow as a percentage of stock-based compensation". Bill Mylod calls stock pay "the most single valuable expense". No specific past example given.
Tech S-Curve Leaders|A10|Little dilution: Bill Mylod states that a shrinking share count turns business growth into a bigger share-price gain, because "if the enterprise value has doubled, the share price has tripled" for a company that bought back stock. No specific past example given.
Tech S-Curve Leaders|A11|Self-funded: Maverick states that today's AI build-out differs from the dot-com one because spending is "well under 100 percent" of operating cash flow. Gavin Baker asks whether spending is "funded out of debt or cash flows", and Bill Gurley warns that a "three to one ... debt to equity ratio" could be "a real painful ... downside". A mentioned example: the dot-com build-out versus today's cash-funded AI build-out.
Tech S-Curve Leaders|A12|Return on new c: Bill Gurley states that growth spending must be judged by "what's the return on the incremental investment". Michael Mauboussin states that growth creates value only when companies "earn above the opportunity cost of capital". No specific past example given.
Tech S-Curve Leaders|A13|Working capital: Bill Gurley states that slipping receivables mean a company is pulling revenue forward, because "their DSO's are just slipping out". Gavin Baker states that piling inventory signals a bust, because before the 2000 chip crash "customer inventories and days inventory were at all-time highs". A mentioned example: chip stocks in 2000.
Tech S-Curve Leaders|A14|Size (market ca: Big enough to trade without moving the price. No specific past example given.
Tech S-Curve Leaders|A15|Liquidity: Must be able to build and exit a position. No specific past example given.
Tech S-Curve Leaders|A16|Valuation: Bill Gurley states that a high sales multiple needs high growth, because "if you want a 10x multiple you got be growing 30 35%". Leon Shaulov warns that winners "may not screen as the cheapest things in the world", so failing only this rule makes a 'wait for a better price' near miss. No specific past example given.
Tech S-Curve Leaders|J|Human / AI review: Alex Sacerdote states that without a moat "you're a zero", and that he sells as adoption reaches about 30-40% of the market (the S-curve stage). Bill Gurley states that compute depreciation needs a look, because "servers typically depreciate a bit like fish". Market position, net retention, AI share of sales, customer concentration and China/Taiwan exposure were left out of the screen by choice. No specific past example given.
